item.title: It’s Time for Peacock’s Annual Price Increase. Here’s What You Need to Know.
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Peacock just applied its annual price increase to your subscription. How much do you have to pay now? Read on to find out.
item.content:encoded:
Peacock’s latest price increase hit this week

If you’ve been looking to sign up for Peacock this week, you might have noticed that the site prices differ from what third party guides and news sites claim. That’s because Peacock just raised its prices for new members, effective August 18. 2026. Existing customers will see this price increase on their next bill on or after September 17, 2026. So how much more will a Peacock subscription cost you, and is it worth it? Let’s dive into the details and find out.

Keep up with all the latest in entertainment news

Subscribe to CableTV.com's email newsletter for the latest TV event viewing guides, entertaining takes, and money-saving promotions.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

How much does Peacock cost in 2026?

After the August 2026 price increase, a Peacock subscription will cost you anywhere between $8.99/mo. and $19.99/mo.

Peacock Monthly Prices

New price Old price Full Peacock library Ad-free? Live NBC?
Peacock Select $8.99/mo. $7.99/mo. — — —
Peacock Premium $12.99/mo. $10.99/mo. ✔ — —
Peacock Premium Plus $19.99/mo. $16.99/mo. ✔ ✔ ✔
Peacock’s lowest tier, Peacock Select, is going up by $1/mo. Its middle tier, Peacock Premium, is going up by $2/mo. And its highest tier, the ad-free Peacock Premium Plus, is going up by $3/mo. These changes went into effect on August 18, 2026. Existing customers will see these prices reflected on their bills beginning September 17, 2026. Peacock’s annual prices are also going up, although they’re staying on pace with the monthly prices. It’s very common for 12-month plans to cost the same as 10 months at the monthly rate.

Peacock Annual Prices

New price Old price Full Peacock library Ad-free? Live NBC?
Peacock Select $89.99/mo. $79.99/mo. — — —
Peacock Premium $129.99/mo. $109.99/mo. ✔ — —
Peacock Premium Plus $199.99/mo. $169.99/mo. ✔ ✔ ✔
So is this new price increase reasonable? Peacock’s last price increase took effect in July 2025, which seems like just yesterday. But these days, most streaming services do raise their prices every year. It’s an unfortunate reality of the industry. Still, a three-dollar price increase on the only ad-free plan is pretty drastic — especially since it rose the same amount last year. It’s hard to believe that the Premium Plus plan has doubled in price (from $9.99/mo. to $19.99/mo.) since 2022. Peacock Premium is still the best way to get the streaming service (unless you can get a deal through another bundle or cable provider). Peacock Select’s price may be tempting, but its library is extremely limited compared to the pricier plans. Peacock Select customers lose out on live sports, movies, and Peacock Originals. Unfortunately, picking the best Peacock plan may mean you have to put up with ads. Unless you’re okay with that new, shocking price tag.

Peacock

Peacock has come a long way from the free service it was when it debuted back in 2020. It’s a pretty pricey option now, but we generally feel that it has the content to back it up — especially for sports fans.

item.title: Every Netflix, HBO Max, and Hulu Price Increase: The History of Streaming Service Prices
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: I’ve compiled data on all of our favorite streaming services to see the bigger picture. Which services are making reasonable changes, and which are taking advantage of economic panic?
item.content:encoded:
It’s not just you; streaming prices are rising, fast

Almost every major streaming service has increased its prices several times in the last few years. It’s gotten to the point where yearly price hikes feel like the norm, but it’s easy to forget that it wasn’t always like this. Streaming used to be a cheap, dependable form of entertainment. Prices would stay steady for years at a time. But those days are over. We love streaming television here at CableTV.com, but we also want to hold entertainment platforms and conglomerates accountable. So I’ve compiled data on all of our favorite streaming services to see the bigger picture. Which streaming price increases are reasonable changes, and which are taking advantage of economic panic? Let’s find out.

Why trust us? Despite our company name, we love television in all its forms. (Cable-and-streaming-TV-dot-com just wouldn’t have the same ring.) Our entertainment experts have spent thousands of hours testing all of the best (and worst) streaming services, and hundreds more hours tracking and researching industry trends. It’s our job to keep an eye on everything the big corporate streamers get up to—so you can focus on enjoying your favorite shows.
Jump to:

Netflix pricing history

Netflix’s latest price increase went into effect in March 2026. Netflix currently offers three plans:

  • Netflix Standard with Ads ($8.99/mo., 2 streams)
  • Netflix Standard ($19.99/mo., 2 streams, no ads)
  • Netflix Premium ($26.99/mo., 4 streams, no ads)

Netflix broke its streaming service off from its DVD rental service in 2011 and stopped renting out DVDs altogether in 2023. Netflix Basic (1 stream) was discontinued in January 2025. All Netflix plans now provide at least two simultaneous streams.

Read More About Netflix

Netflix’s monthly price history

Netflix Basic Netflix Standard with Ads Netflix Standard Netflix Premium
2011 — — $7.99 —
2012 — — $7.99 —
2013 $6.99 — $7.99 $11.99
2014 $7.99 — $8.99 $11.99
2015 $7.99 — $9.99 $11.99
2016 $7.99 — $9.99 $11.99
2017 $8.99 — $10.99 $13.99
2018 $8.99 — $10.99 $13.99
2019 $8.99 — $12.99 $15.99
2020 $8.99 — $13.99 $17.99
2021 $8.99 — $13.99 $17.99
2022 $9.99 — $15.49 $19.99
2023 $11.99 $6.99 $15.49 $22.99
2024 $11.99 $6.99 $15.49 $22.99
2025 — $7.99 $17.99 $24.99
2026 — $8.99 $19.99 $26.99
Netflix’s streaming service began as a free perk for its DVD rental subscribers in 2007, but became a standalone option in 2011. Users could pay $7.99/mo. for Netflix’s full, ad-free library of television and movies. That price for a Standard subscription—that is, two streams and no ads—has steadily increased every few years since its inception. Netflix subscribers now have to make a choice: Pay over double what the original Netflix subscription cost to maintain their ad-free experience, or downgrade to Netflix Standard with Ads for a reasonable $8.99/mo. price tag. Of course, you could always upgrade to Netflix Premium for those coveted four streams. But $26.99/mo. is a lot, even considering inflation, and those four streams don’t guarantee you can share your password with anyone outside of your main household. That’s the hidden fee behind every Netflix subscription: Restricted password sharing. Standard subscribers can purchase one extra member for $6.99–$8.99/mo., and Premium subscribers can purchase two. Got more family members than that? You’re on your own.

Disney+ pricing history

Disney+’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. Disney+ currently offers two plans:

  • Disney+ Basic ($11.99/mo., 4 streams)
  • Disney+ Premium ($18.99/mo., 4 streams, no ads)

Read More About Disney+

Disney+’s monthly price history

Disney+ Basic Disney+ Premium
2019 — $6.99
2020 — $6.99
2021 — $7.99
2022 $7.99 $10.99
2023 $7.99 $13.99
2024 $9.99 $15.99
2025 $11.99 $18.99
2026 $11.99 $18.99
Disney+ launched in 2019 as an ad-free service, but introduced ads in 2022. Subscribers could choose to remove ads, but it would cost $3 more per month. Disney+’s price has risen astronomically since its inception. Where Netflix took about 14 years to double the price of its original plan, Disney+ did the same in just four. Rather than the steady increase over time to mirror inflation, it gives the impression that Disney is scrambling to recover costs (since cancelling and removing a bunch of shows didn’t seem to work). When I recommend Disney+, I’m not usually recommending the standalone streaming service. It just seems like too much money for too little content (unless you’re really passionate about Star Wars). Instead, it’s a much better deal to bundle Disney+ with Disney’s other major streaming service, Hulu. Later in 2026, this will be your only option to watch Hulu content, anyway (keep reading for more on that).

Hulu pricing history

Hulu’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. Hulu currently offers two (on-demand) plans:

  • Hulu Basic ($11.99/mo., 2 streams)
  • Hulu Premium ($18.99/mo., 2 streams, no ads)

Read More About Hulu

Hulu’s monthly price history

Hulu Basic Hulu Premium
2010 $7.99 —
2011 $7.99 —
2012 $7.99 —
2013 $7.99 —
2014 $7.99 —
2015 $7.99 $11.99
2016 $7.99 $11.99
2017 $7.99 $11.99
2018 $7.99 $11.99
2019 $5.99 $11.99
2020 $5.99 $11.99
2021 $6.99 $12.99
2022 $7.99 $14.99
2023 $7.99 $17.99
2024 $9.99 $18.99
2025 $11.99 $18.99
2026 $11.99 $18.99
Hulu was pretty chill about price increases for a long time. For its first eight years of existence, its plans stayed exactly the same. And since Hulu began as an ad-supported service rather than an ad-free one, the introduction of different price tiers didn’t feel like a total betrayal. But then Disney bought a majority stake in Hulu in 2019 and finished acquiring the service entirely in 2023. Since then, standalone prices—especially for Hulu Premium— have steadily increased, likely as an incentive to make users switch over to the Disney Bundle. In early 2025, I predicted that Disney would shut down Hulu as a standalone app and permanently merge it with Disney+. And guess what? I was right! You can expect the price of Disney+ to go up dramatically in late 2026 (likely in October) as they make the move official.

The Disney Bundle pricing history

The Disney Bundle’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. There are currently several ways to get The Disney Bundle. Here are the ones we’re tracking:

  • Duo Basic ($12.99/mo., Hulu and Disney+)
  • Duo Premium ($19.99/mo., Hulu and Disney+, no ads)
  • Trio Basic ($19.99/mo., Hulu, Disney+, and ESPN Select)
  • Trio Premium ($29.99/mo., Hulu, Disney+, and ESPN Select, no ads)

The Legacy Disney Bundle ($24.99/mo., Hulu, Disney+, and ESPN Select, no ads on Disney+) is only available to existing subscribers.

Read More About The Disney Bundle

The Disney Bundle’s monthly price history

Legacy Disney Bundle Duo Basic Duo Premium Trio Basic Trio Premium
2019 $12.99 — — — —
2020 $12.99 — — — —
2021 $13.99 — — — —
2022 $14.99 $9.99 — $12.99 $19.99
2023 $18.99 $9.99 $19.99 $14.99 $24.99
2024 $21.99 $10.99 $19.99 $16.99 $26.99
2025 $24.99 $12.99 $19.99 $19.99 $29.99
2026 $24.99 $12.99 $19.99 $19.99 $29.99
The Disney Bundle is a great way to get multiple streaming services for cheap—if you’re okay with ads. The Duo Premium and Trio Premium plans are pretty pricey in their own right, even if they’re technically better deals than subscribing to every service individually. In my opinion, the gap between the Basic and Premium prices is way too high. Disney Bundle subscribers can also now access Hulu through Disney+’s interface. You can expect to see more changes in (likely October) 2026 when Disney finally shuts down Hulu as a standalone app and makes the Disney Bundle its biggest priority.

HBO Max pricing history

Max’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. Max currently offers three plans:

  • HBO Max Basic with Ads ($10.99/mo., 2 streams)
  • HBO Max Standard ($18.49/mo., 2 streams, no ads)
  • HBO Max Premium ($22.99/mo., 4 streams, no ads)

HBO Max changed its name to Max in 2023 and changed it back to HBO Max in Summer 2025.

Read More About HBO Max

HBO Max’s monthly price history

HBO Max Basic with Ads HBO Max Standard HBO Max Premium
2020 — $14.99 —
2021 $9.99 $14.99 —
2022 $9.99 $14.99 —
2023 $9.99 $15.99 $19.99
2024 $9.99 $16.99 $20.99
2025 $10.99 $18.49 $22.99
2026 $10.99 $18.49 $22.99
When HBO Max launched in 2020, it was already pretty expensive. That’s because it couldn’t be cheaper than the HBO cable channel, a premium add-on with a premium price tag, or its streaming predecessor, HBO Now, which only streamed HBO content. So unlike Disney+ and Peacock, HBO Max never had the chance to market itself as the cool, cheap, cable alternative. Instead, it began as a way for non-cable subscribers to watch WarnerMedia-owned content on demand. The “HBO” brand name promised high-quality, prestige entertainment and was bolstered by a library full of titles from all of WarnerMedia’s brands: DC, Turner Classic Movies, Cartoon Network, Adult Swim, Studio Ghibli, and more. But things went downhill after WarnerMedia merged with Discovery to form Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD). The two media giants’ streaming services, HBO Max and Discovery+, merged into the monosyllabic “Max.” Max lost its premium cable identity when it lost its HBO branding, and the platform was flooded with Discovery’s most popular reality shows. (Discovery+ continues to this day as a standalone service that features dozens of additional reality TV franchises and spinoffs.) Something really bothers me about the name change—WBD justified it with the claim that the HBO branding was scaring parents away. WBD wanted to welcome kids onto their platform. This should have been a slam dunk because WBD owns Cartoon Network. But instead of investing in animation and kids’ content, Max slowly removed popular CN titles from its library. WBD reduced spending on animation, shut down CN’s physical headquarters, and stripped away the station’s identity. Kids lost interest in Max. In 2025, WBD gave up on kids. It sold off “Sesame Street” to Netflix and “The Amazing World of Gumball” to Hulu, put the “HBO” back in “HBO Max,” and is desperately trying to claw back its standing as the place to find serious adult television.

Amazon Prime Video pricing history

Prime Video’s latest price increase went into effect in April 2026. You can choose to subscribe to Amazon Prime Video on its own:

  • Amazon Prime Video ($8.99/mo., 3 streams)

Or bundle it with a full Amazon Prime membership:

  • Amazon Prime ($14.99/mo., 3 streams)

Prime Video was ad-free until January 2024, when it put ads on most of its content. Amazon Prime Ultra is an add-on that costs $4.99/mo., and removes ads from most Prime content.

Read More About Prime Video

Amazon Prime Video’s monthly price history

Amazon Prime Video (ads) Amazon Prime Video (no ads) Amazon Prime (ads) Amazon Prime (no ads)
2016 — $8.99 — $10.99
2017 — $8.99 — $10.99
2018 — $8.99 — $12.99
2019 — $8.99 — $12.99
2020 — $8.99 — $12.99
2021 — $8.99 — $12.99
2022 — $8.99 — $14.99
2023 — $8.99 — $14.99
2024 $8.99 $11.98 $14.99 $17.98
2025 $8.99 $11.98 $14.99 $17.98
2026 $8.99 $13.98 $14.99 $19.98
Amazon Prime Video’s pricing structure was pretty reasonable until 2024. Customers could access the service either by subscribing to the full Amazon Prime membership (for free two-day shipping and more) or by subscribing to Prime Video as a standalone service. But Amazon ruffled a lot of feathers in 2024 by putting ads on all of its content, not just the titles it inherited from the now-defunct free ad-supported television (FAST) service Freevee. If customers hate the frequent interruptions, they can remove them with Amazon Prime Video Ultra, which is an additional $4.99/mo. fee on top of the regular subscription. Even though Amazon doesn’t advertise it this way, I consider this to be a new pricing tier, so I’ve written it up in the table above accordingly. Prime Video took a page out of Disney+’s playbook: get customers hooked on ad-free television and then take it away, hiding the privilege behind another paywall. It’s a transparent attempt to wring more money out of customers, and I’m not a fan.

Apple TV pricing history

Apple TV’s latest price increase went into effect in August 2025. Apple TV currently offers one plan:

  • Apple TV ($12.99/mo., 6 streams, no ads)

Read More About Apple TV+

Apple TV’s monthly price history

Apple TV
2019 $4.99
2020 $4.99
2021 $4.99
2022 $6.99
2023 $9.99
2024 $9.99
2025 $12.99
2026 $12.99
Apple TV’s price history is easy to track because it’s only ever offered one plan. And that plan has only gone up in price three times in the platform’s history. It’s surprising that Apple TV has never imitated the multiple-tier-cash-grabs of its competitors, but that’s why I always rate the service so highly. I find a lot of other streaming services’ pricing schemes to be anti-consumer. I’m hesitant to praise Apple TV too much for keeping its plans cheap and simple. Soon after I praised Prime Video for doing the same in 2023, Amazon decided to charge customers an extra $2.99/mo. for the same ad-free service they’d always gotten. And then there’s the whole debacle of its 2025 rebrand from “Apple TV+” to “Apple TV.” But Apple TV’s content library is almost entirely original. Maybe the lack of licensing fees will keep prices low (and advertising far, far away) for a little while longer.

Paramount+ pricing history

Paramount+’s latest price increase went into effect in January 2026. Paramount+ currently offers two plans:

  • Paramount+ Essential ($8.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • Paramount+ Premium ($13.99/mo., 3 streams, no ads)

Paramount+ Premium was discontinued in 2023 when it was replaced by the newly discounted Paramount+ with SHOWTIME bundle. The Paramount+ with SHOWTIME bundle was then renamed to Paramount+ Premium in 2025.

Read More About Paramount+

Paramount+’s monthly price history

Paramount+ Essential Paramount+ Premium Paramount+ with SHOWTIME
2021 $4.99 $9.99 —
2022 $4.99 $9.99 $14.99
2023 $5.99 — $11.99
2024 $7.99 — $12.99
2025 $7.99 $12.99 $12.99
2026 $8.99 $13.99 —
Paramount+ is an interesting case because its premium tier offers two streaming services in one. Unlike other streaming bundles, you can’t subscribe to both components of Paramount+ with SHOWTIME separately. SHOWTIME no longer exists as its own entity, and even the premium cable channel is called Paramount+ with SHOWTIME now. Paramount+ with SHOWTIME is cheaper now than when the bundle first debuted in 2022. In a remarkably reasonable decision, the company split the difference between the $14.99/mo. bundle price and the $9.99/mo. price of the Premium plan it was replacing. It’s rare to see a streaming service decrease the price of one of its plans over time—especially without taking something important away. The only other instance that comes to mind is when Hulu decreased its prices in 2019 in an attempt to pull customers away from its notoriously expensive competitor, Netflix. And because nothing can be simple with Paramount+: the Paramount+ with SHOWTIME tier is now called Paramount+ Premium. But it’s not the same Paramount+ Premium that the company offered in 2022; this time, it comes with SHOWTIME content. It’s just not in the name anymore. Forget SHOWTIME exists, actually. That branding is so 2024.

Peacock pricing history

Peacock’s latest price increase went into effect in August 2026. Peacock currently offers three plans:

  • Peacock Select ($8.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • Peacock Premium ($12.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • Peacock Premium Plus ($19.99/mo., 3 streams, no ads)

Peacock discontinued its free tier in 2023.

Read More About Peacock

Peacock’s monthly price history

Peacock Select Peacock Premium Peacock Premium Plus
2020 — $4.99 $9.99
2021 — $4.99 $9.99
2022 — $4.99 $9.99
2023 — $5.99 $11.99
2024 — $7.99 $13.99
2025 $7.99 $10.99 $16.99
2026 $8.99 $12.99 $19.99
Peacock’s plan names have never made too much sense. Most streaming services use “Premium” to mean “ad-free,” but not Peacock. At Peacock, the only way you’re getting rid of ads is by subscribing to Premium Plus. This whole naming scheme is probably because Peacock used to offer a free tier when it was first starting out, but it was discontinued in 2023. Nowadays, instead of a free tier, the thriftiest Peacock plan is called Peacock Select. Like Premium, it has ads, but it doesn’t allow access to a lot of Peacock’s library. You’ll miss out on originals, sports, and movies—Peacock’s three biggest strengths. But you can still enjoy old episodes of “The Office,” I guess.

ESPN pricing history

ESPN’s latest price increase went into effect in August 2025. ESPN currently offers two plans:

  • ESPN Select ($11.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • ESPN Unlimited ($29.99/mo., 3 streams)

ESPN  subscriptions are only available with ads. ESPN Select is the new name of ESPN+, and ESPN Unlimited is a new plan introduced in 2025.

Read More About ESPN+

ESPN+’s monthly price history

ESPN Select ESPN Unlimited
2018 $4.99 —
2019 $4.99 —
2020 $5.99 —
2021 $6.99 —
2022 $9.99 —
2023 $10.99 —
2024 $11.99 —
2025 $11.99 $29.99
2026 $11.99 $29.99
Unlike my colleague Taylor Kujawa, I’m not much of a sports fan beyond the occasional baseball game, so ESPN+’s new subscription system was initially pretty confusing to me. Essentially, the ESPN+ streaming service still exists, it’s just been rebranded as ESPN Select. Superfans can upgrade to the $29.99/mo. ESPN Unlimited plan for even more sports content, like the ESPN, ESPN2, and ESPNU cable channels. Previously, ESPN+ did not include everything airing on ESPN the cable channel. “For customers, ESPN’s unlimited direct-to-consumer service is a double-edged sword,” says CableTV.com Sports Editor Taylor Kujawa. “It’s perfect for fans of the ESPN brand and the sports covered under ESPN’s media agreements. But the rise of these standalone streaming services could make watching sports much more expensive than it already is.” Both of theses new plans are part of a larger service called simply “ESPN,” not to be confused with the ESPN cable channel.

Crunchyroll pricing history

Crunchyroll’s latest price increase went into effect in January 2026. Crunchyroll currently offers three paid tiers:

  • Crunchyroll Fan ($9.99/mo., 1 stream)
  • Crunchyroll Mega Fan ($13.99/mo., 4 streams, game vault)
  • Crunchyroll Ultimate Fan ($17.99/mo., 6 streams, game vault, manga)

Crunchyroll discontinued its free tier at the end of 2025.

Read More About Crunchyroll

Crunchyroll’s monthly price history

Crunchyroll Fan Crunchyroll Mega Fan Crunchyroll Ultimate Fan
2009 $6.95 —
2010 $6.95 — —
2011 $6.95 — —
2012 $6.95 — —
2013 $6.95 — —
2014 $6.95 — —
2015 $6.95 — —
2016 $6.95 — —
2017 $6.95 — —
2018 $6.95 — —
2019 $6.95 — —
2020 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2021 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2022 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2023 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2024 $7.99 $11.99 $15.99
2025 $7.99 $11.99 $15.99
2026 $9.99 $13.99 $17.99
Crunchyroll began as a free service in 2006, and initially, memberships were more of a donation thing to keep the site running. Users would pay for higher-quality streaming and the privilege of a star-shaped badge. Crunchyroll started formally offering a premium membership by 2009. This predates Netflix’s streaming service; there was no blueprint for how these subscriptions should work. In addition to the standard credit card and PayPal payment methods, users could also pay for their memberships by physically putting a check in an envelope and sending it through the mail. It was a different era. Early Crunchyroll memberships would give members same-day simulcasts and access to 100% of Crunchyroll’s library. Free users would get simulcasts a week late, and access to “most” of Crunchyroll’s library. It’s hard to say exactly how much “most” is, and how that percentage has changed over time. Unlike today, there weren’t a lot of online news articles documenting streaming service policy changes in 2009. I’m getting a lot of my info by crawling through janky captures on the Internet Archive.Over the past several years, Crunchyroll put more and more of its content behind a paywall until it finally discontinued the free subscription entirely at the end of 2025. As of January 2026, if you want to watch anything on Crunchyroll, you’ll need a paid account, just like any other streaming service. When you compare Crunchyroll to other streaming services, you realize it’s actually still a pretty good deal. None of its paid tiers have ads, and you get the full anime experience for a relatively low price. The higher tiers are just nice-to-haves, with bonus perks like video games and manga. Crunchyroll’s subscriber count has been booming in recent years, so this paywall strategy seems to be working for them. But it’s still disappointing to see something that used to be free jump up to ten dollars a month.

item.content:encoded:
A weekend full of Disney headlines

Disney dazzled audiences this weekend with its Disney Entertainment Showcase at D23, its annual convention. For those lucky enough to be in the Honda Center, they were treated to musical numbers and sneak peaks from all sorts of upcoming Disney properties. The rest of us will have to wait until the movies come out in 2027, 2028, and beyond…. But we can still enjoy certain teasers and clips from the show. I’ve compiled a roundup of what I consider the biggest news to come out of D23 this year. Ready? Let’s get started!

“The Bluey Movie”

At long last, “The Bluey Movie” has a teaser trailer. The film, inspired by the super-popular kids’ show, was first announced in 2024. We don’t know a ton about the movie’s plot, but the teaser trailer shows off a brand new 3D art style for the little blue dog and her sister. The movie will come to theaters on August 6, 2027, and will likely appear on Disney+ several months after that. Oh, and don’t worry Australians — you’ll be able to stream it as well.

Good news for “Kingdom Hearts” fans

I spend a lot of time researching upcoming animated series, and this is one I’m super excited for. “Kingdom Hearts” is a popular video game series that mixes “Final Fantasy” with iconic Disney characters like Donald, Mickey, and Goofy. Since the Disney mobile game “Twisted Wonderland” got an anime adaptation last year, it was only a matter of time before “Kingdom Hearts” got its own show, too. The “Kingdom Hearts” show will premiere on Disney Channel and Disney+, but does not yet have a release date.And that’s not the only “Kingdom Hearts” news to come out of D23 this year. “Kingdom Hearts IV” got a new trailer, featuring a look at the game’s new “Coco”-inspired world. “Kingdom Hearts IV” will come to Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S in late 2027.

Keep up with all the latest in entertainment news

Subscribe to CableTV.com's email newsletter for the latest TV event viewing guides, entertaining takes, and money-saving promotions.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

New Pixar films

Do you like sequels? Disney’s got sequels. We got a first look at two new Pixar sequels this D23: “Incredibles 3” and “Coco 2.” “Incredibles 3” will focus on the Parr kids: Violet, Jack-Jack, and Dash. This time, the siblings will be taking on a new and powerful supervillain. It doesn’t seem like they’ve aged that much in the last 22 years, which isn’t much of a surprise since executive producer Brad Bird has said that it’s important to him that the trio remain children. “Incredibles 3” will come to theaters on June 16, 2028. Miguel, on the other hand, has aged. The new “Coco 2” concept art shows Miguel as a teenager, and his would-be grandfather Ernesto de la Cruz as a more bedraggled, menacing version of himself. “Coco 2” will come to theaters in November 2029.And if sequels aren’t your thing, you can still look forward to the upcoming, original Pixar film, “Ghost Market.” It’s Pixar’s first horror film, but it’s “not like some of those other scary movies.” The first teaser trailer, which you can watch above, shows a ghost enjoying a bowl of ramen. And now I’m hungry. “Ghost Market” will come to theaters in Spring 2028.

Disney Princesses are back in the spotlight

Disney Princesses are having a moment right now. If you didn’t know, World Princess Week began on August 16, and will run until August 22. Disney+ is celebrating with a wave of new content, including a filmed concert featuring Disney Princesses past and present.But as for Disney Princesses of the future? Fans can look forward to “Frozen 3,” which was heavily promoted at this year’s conference. Attendees saw an exclusive clip from the film, showing Elsa pulling Anna away from her and Kristoff’s wedding to investigate a mysterious new ice queen. And some of the actors made an appearance to sing new songs from the film. “Frozen 3” will come to theaters in Fall 2027.Meanwhile, on the live-action side of things, fans were treated to a video message from Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim, stars of the new live-action “Tangled” film. They’re filming in Spain right now, so the message showed them in full costume travelling around the real Spanish buildings Disney is using to represent the kingdom of Corona. “Tangled” will come to theaters on March 31, 2028.

You’ll be able to watch all of these new titles and more on Disney+ sometime in the distant future. In the meantime, there are plenty of Disney and Pixar movies you can watch while you wait.

item.title: Spectrum-Cox Merger Finalized: What Happens Next to Your Cable Plan
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Charter Communications and Cox will officially merge after state regulators gave their approval. Here’s what happens next.
item.content:encoded:
Long-awaited merger reaches finish line

The Spectrum-Cox merger is finally done. California state regulators approved Charter Communications’ $34.5 billion purchase of Cox Communications last week, clearing the way for Spectrum’s acquisition of Cox to officially create the nation’s largest cable services provider. The newly combined company will service nearly 37 million customers nationwide and cover more than 70 million locations. The FCC approved the deal in late February, and both providers announced their plans to merge in May 2025.

Stay tuned with CableTV.com

Get the latest deals, show premieres, and more by signing up for our newsletter.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

What happens next with Spectrum-Cox

Amid a run of internet mergers, Spectrum-Cox was one of the biggest shoes to drop in recent months. Let’s break down what’ll happen to your cable service now that Spectrum and Cox have finally finished their merger.

Expect changes for Cox customers, Spectrum customers (mostly) unfazed

As we previously highlighted, Cox Communications will be the new name of the combined parent company, while Spectrum will be the face of its home internet, TV, and phone services. Spectrum customers won’t experience any major changes, while Cox will transition over to Spectrum’s pricing, services, and customer management system in the coming months. Spectrum’s exact integration plans have yet to be finalized, so it’s unclear how issues like plan-level price differences and Spectrum TV’s bundled streaming services will be handled for former Cox customers. Still, we expect that Cox’s branded services — like Cox Mobile and Contour TV — will be replaced by Spectrum alternatives like Spectrum Mobile. Similarly, new customers in Cox’s footprint will get Spectrum’s plans, bundle options, and pricing. We’re especially interested to see how Spectrum handles Spectrum’s pricing differences for current Cox customers. For example, a 500 Mbps plan starts at $40 for Spectrum and $85 for Cox customers. We’d wager that Spectrum will simply “grandfather” existing Cox customers over to Spectrum at their current rate, but give the option to transfer pricing for anyone who raises a stink about it. (That said, it’s not all bad news—Spectrum also announced that Cox TV subscribers in the Los Angeles Dodgers broadcast area will get Spectrum’s SportsNet LA channel for no additional cost.) These changes also apply to Cox and Spectrum employees — via Cord Cutters News, they’ve reportedly been told the company’s post-merger start date will be on August 20.

Could Spectrum-Xfinity be the next merger?

The name of the game in the telco space has been consolidation, as the recent wave of mergers has whittled the nationwide cable market down to a two-company race between Comcast and Charter. (AT&T and Verizon are the only comparable national providers, though both focus more on fiber and mobile services.) Unlike Spectrum-Cox, Charter and Xfinity have significant footprint overlap across the United States and virtually identical service catalogs (internet, TV, and phone). Given the number of ISPs that have joined up instead of fighting for market share, it’s no wonder that numerous analysts have speculated about Comcast and Spectrum being the next big merger. Not only that, but Comcast’s June announcement that it split up its internet and TV divisions into separate companies added more fuel to the fire. Though Comcast executives denied that the move meant they were open for business, the FCC’s willingness to rubber-stamp mergers means that we can’t rule out the possibility of Xfinity-Spectrum happening. That said, state regulators have been willing to gum up the works in Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros., and the prospect of a single national cable ISP could invite similar scrutiny. We’ll have more information as the situation develops, so stay tuned.

Students get exclusive discounts on streaming services

What’s the value of a college degree? Does it give you better job opportunities or broaden your academic horizons? None of that really matters—the important part is that it gets you a couple dollars off of subscription services. And those dollars add up! Some only allow four years of savings, while others let you stay for as long as you’re enrolled (even if you graduate late). And Amazon breaks the mold by offering discounts to all young adults, not just those attending university. Don’t qualify for student discounts? Try annual billing

The trick to getting discounted Apple TV is actually to sign up for Apple Music Student. As a longtime Spotify user, I deleted Apple Music from my iPad a long time ago, so it took me a minute to redownload the app. At first, I thought I was in the wrong place because I only saw my old iTunes library (I’ll never escape U2’s Songs of Innocence). During the process, it may seem like you’re only signing up for Apple Music, but as long as you’re getting the discounted rate ($6.99/mo.), you’ll get Apple TV as well. Since I graduated from college several years ago, I usually can’t get too far into the sign-up process for student discounts. But Apple’s verification process seems to work with any student login credentials, even for me, a long-graduated alum, so I’ve created a step-by-step guide to help you through this (frankly, confusing) process.

How to get discounted Apple TV as a college student with an iPad

  1. Download Apple Music from the App Store if you haven’t already. Open Apple Music.
  2. Click on the red “Get 1 month of free music” banner.
    1. If no banner shows up, click on the user icon in the top right to open the account menu.
    2. Then, click on “Get 1 Month Free.”
  3. When prompted, select “See All Plans.”
  4. Scroll down to “College Student.”
  5. Click on “Verify Student Status.”

    1. If you’ve verified your student status in the past, you might skip this window and go right to Step 8.
  7. In the pop-up window, enter your school log-in credentials. For me, this was the same username and password I used for anything Cornell-related (e.g., email, class registration, etc.).
  8. Verify in the Apple payment window that you’re subscribing to Apple Music Student with a 1-mo. free trial and a $6.99/mo. charge.
    1. Note the renewal date if you plan on canceling before your 1st payment. You’ll need to cancel at least a day before that date.
  9. Follow the on-screen instructions to confirm your payment. For me, I double-click my power button to confirm app downloads.

item.content:encoded:
How many national TV games does each NBA team have in 2026-2027?

The NBA released its full schedule for the 2026-2027 season on Thursday. There are plenty of intriguing stretches that fans will want to mark on their calendars, including games on Christmas Day and MLK Day, plus the NBA Cup.

But when it comes to the day-to-day grind of the NBA season, there are 82 games per team to keep track of. And if you’re a fan who loves more than one team — or someone who doesn’t have access to a local TV station — the national TV games are arguably the simplest way to consume the league.

So we thought it’d be handy to map out all 30 NBA teams and how many national TV games each has during the 2026-2027 season. A reminder: These counts are subject to change depending on how well or poorly a team performs throughout the season.

Highlights of the NBA schedule release

The NBA schedule release is like Christmas morning for any avid NBA fan — myself included. There’s nothing like breaking down Opening Night, long road trips, rivalry matchups, and the home stretch before the playoffs.

While it would be impossible to break down the schedule for every single NBA team — that’s 1,230 total games, mind you — here are some things I found interesting through the lens of how many national TV games each team got.

  • Big markets are king, but a Finals team gets rewarded. The Lakers and Knicks each got the max number of national games allotted this season at 34. But so did the Spurs, who play in a traditionally small market. It just goes to show that winning matters, too.
  • Sucks to suck, Brooklyn. The Nets got just two games on national TV this season, despite playing in a huge market. But the team is bad, and it has long played second fiddle to the Knicks in New York.
  • No Giannis, no coverage. The Milwaukee Bucks find themselves back in small-market territory after Giannis Antetokounmpo left for Miami. Without him, the Bucks have only two national TV games on the initial schedule.
  • Nuggets and Warriors beat Boston. Star power matters when it comes to national TV games in the NBA. So it’s not really a surprise that teams led by Nikola Jokic and Steph Curry get nearly 30 national games. But the Celtics got one fewer than both, and I would argue they have a better chance of winning it all than either team.
  • LeBron. The 76ers were one of four teams to get the maximum 34 national games. LeBron James chose the Sixers in free agency. Enough said.

item.description: Score a free season of NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube and YouTube TV courtesy of Verizon. Here’s how to claim the deal before football season kicks off.
item.content:encoded:
Verizon’s giving away NFL Sunday Ticket for free

With the NFL preseason starting up, it’s time for football fans to lock in how they’ll be tuning into the 2026 NFL regular season. NFL Sunday Ticket, the service that streams every out-of-market Sunday game of the season, has become an essential part of any serious fan’s football-watching arsenal. However, shelling out hundreds of dollars ($480 to be exact) for a subscription isn’t quite as fun as tuning into your favorite team. Thankfully, Verizon has dropped a major deal to keep some extra cash in your wallet this season. From now until September 23, new customers who sign up for Verizon Home Internet can get NFL Sunday Ticket at no additional cost. Already locked into an internet plan? No worries. Until that same date, new and current Verizon Wireless customers can also claim free NFL Sunday Ticket by purchasing an eligible 5G phone and signing up for (or upgrading to) an Unlimited plan. Keep reading for more details on how to snag these free NFL Sunday Ticket deals today.

How to claim your free NFL Sunday Ticket subscription

There are two ways to claim a free NFL Sunday Ticket subscription from Verizon: by signing up for a new internet plan, or by purchasing a new phone and upgrading to an Unlimited plan. The terms change depending on whether you’re a new or existing Verizon customer, and there’s a bit of fine print to sift through, so let me break the deals down so you can choose which route is best for you.

Get NFL Sunday Ticket with Verizon Home Internet (new customers only)

New Verizon Home Internet customers must sign up for and maintain one of the following internet plans:

  • Verizon 5G Home Ultimate plan
  • Verizon Home Internet Lite Extra plan
  • Verizon Fios 1 Gig or higher plan

Get NFL Sunday Ticket with Verizon Wireless (new or existing customers)

  • New customers: Must purchase an eligible 5G phone and activate a new smartphone line on an Unlimited Ultimate or Unlimited Plus plan
  • Existing customers: Must purchase an eligible 5G phone and upgrade an existing line to (or activate a new smartphone line on) an Unlimited Ultimate or Unlimited Plus plan
Remember, these NFL Sunday Ticket deals expire on September 23. That feels like a ways off, but time flies—don’t let them fall off your radar before the regular season heats up.
Already a Verizon customer? Don’t worry, current customers who don’t want to purchase a new phone aren’t entirely left out in the cold. Existing Verizon Home Internet and myPlan customers can get NFL Sunday Ticket for $234, a savings of $246. This deal ends a bit sooner, though—September 2—so click the button below to get started.

item.title: New ‘Dimension 20’ Main Cast Season Revealed: Toylight
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Wondering who the cast is for the upcoming Dimension 20 season? Want to know more about ‘Dimension 20: Toylight?’ Keep reading.
item.content:encoded:
The Intrepid Heroes return as wooden toys, dollies, and stuffies

Comedy streaming service Dropout released the trailer for its new “Dimension 20” season, titled “Toylight,” this afternoon. “Dimension 20” is an anthology TTRPG actual play show featuring a new campaign setting every season, often rotating between different casts and game systems. The “Dimension 20” YouTube channel teased the release back in July with a cryptic video titled “Playtime Is Over.” The teaser juxtaposed vintage wartime footage with unsettling black-and-white toys, and we finally know why. The new season, premiering September 16 on Dropout, is about a band of toys trying to keep a dying child from losing their spark of imagination. That spark is called the Toylight, and the Intrepid Heroes must protect it from a harsh world of brightly colored warfare. Want to know more about the new “Dimension 20” season? Watch the trailer below, and read on for everything we know right now!

How to watch “Dimension 20: Toylight”

The first episode of “Dimension 20: Toylight” will premiere on Dropout on September 16. New episodes — of which there are six in total— will air weekly on Wednesday nights. 7:00 p.m. ET, to be precise. You’ll need a Dropout subscription if you want to watch the full season, but Dropout does eventually end up putting season premieres up on the Dimension 20 YouTube channel for free. However, you’ll have to wait until September 23 for the upload. I highly recommend getting a Dropout subscription. They’re not paying me to say that, I just think it’s a good value. And right now you can get 20% off your first year with the promo code FULLYEAR20.

“Dimension 20: Toylight” cast

”Dimension 20: Toylight” is an Intrepid Heroes season, which means it uses the main cast that viewers will recognize from seasons like “Fantasy High” and “A Crown of Candy.” As always with Intrepid Heroes seasons, Brennan Lee Mulligan will DM. He will be using the 2024 version of D&D. According to the new trailer, the cast is:

  • Brian Murphy as Ol’ Clyde Horsey
  • Emily Axford as Tiddleywinks/Cutie Pie
  • Lou Wilson as Wyon
  • Zac Oyama as Avery Augustusus Archibald Tinsley
  • Siobhan Thompson as Constance
  • Ally Beardsley as Calypso

It’s unusual for the show to air two Intrepid Heroes seasons back-to-back, but Dropout is breaking the mold this year with slightly shorter seasons. “Dimension 20: City Council of Darkness,” the show’s Vampire: The Masquerade season featuring the Intrepid Heroes, just ended in July after 14 episodes. “Toylight” will only be six episodes long, bringing this year’s Intrepid Heroes episode count to 20. Intrepid Heroes seasons are usually about 20 episodes long.

The best streaming services for D&D fans

Dropout

If you’re interested at all in D&D actual play, you’ve got to check out Dropout. It’s the exclusive home for every Dimension 20 season, with every installment bigger and better than the last.

Prime Video

The other big D&D actual play show, “Critical Role,” has a working relationship with Amazon Prime. Both “Critical Role” animated series are on Prime Video, making it a must-have service for fans.

item.title: The Jonas Brothers Return to Disney With New Video Podcast Ahead of ‘Camp Rock 3’
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: After you catch the Jonas Brothers in “Camp Rock 3,” check out their video podcast “Hey Jonas!” streaming on Disney+.
item.content:encoded:
Disney+ is the best streaming service for Jonas Brothers fans

The Jonas Brothers may have long outgrown their status as teen heartthrobs, establishing themselves as a real-world, adult band, but that doesn’t mean they can’t make time for Disney Channel every now and then. The sibling trio are making a Disney comeback with the premiere of “Camp Rock 3” later this week, but that’s not the only place you’ll be able to catch them. The Jonas Brothers launched a podcast called “Hey Jonas!” back in May. Each episode, they welcome a different special guest, from Seth Meyers to Millie Bobby Brown. If you’re a fan of the brothers or are just nostalgic for their antics on “Jonas” (2009–2010, R.I.P.), this is probably a show you’ll want to hear. Or watch, since it’s a video podcast. Starting later this week, you’ll be able to watch episodes of “Hey Jonas!” through Disney+ alongside all your other favorite Jonas Brothers titles. This is due to a deal that Disney just struck with iHeartMedia to bring several actor-run podcasts to its platform. The deal also includes five other iHeartMedia video podcasts: “Pod Meets World,” “Desperately Devoted,” “Fake Doctors, Real Friends with Zach and Donald,” “StraightioLab,” and “Thanks Dad with Ego Nwodim.” So if you’re looking to follow your favorite actors but haven’t been able to get into podcasts before, this could be a great starting point. Since they’re video podcasts, they feel much more like traditional shows. Want to learn more about “Hey Jonas!”? Keep reading to learn everything we know so far.

How to watch “Hey Jonas!”

”Hey Jonas!” is already available in all of the usual podcast places, including Apple Podcasts and YouTube. But since it’s a video podcast, you might want to watch it along with the rest of your favorite shows. And that’s where Disney+ comes in. Thanks to this new deal between Disney and iHeartMedia, you’ll be able to watch episodes of “Hey Jonas!” on Disney+ starting August 14. If that date sounds familiar, it’s because that’s also the day that “Camp Rock 3” is premiering on Disney+. (It’s actually premiering the day before on the Disney Channel, but Disney Channel titles always come to Disney+ the next day.) It’s not currently clear whether Disney+ will also host the bonus features and other exclusives usually only found on the iHeartRadio app.

Disney+

Disney+ has all of the Disney channel classics you remember from your childhood, plus reboots of franchises like “Wizards of Waverly Place” and, of course, “Camp Rock.”
